cards.title: Write copy at a third-grade reading level
cards.summary: Keep ad and page copy simple enough that readers spend zero effort decoding it, so attention stays on the offer.
cards.use_when: Writing or editing any PDP, landing page, email, advertorial or paid social ad copy where you need faster comprehension and lower bounce.
steps: Draft your copy, then read it back looking for words a third grader would stumble on — multi-syllable abstractions, jargon, industry terms, long clause chains.
Replace those with plain-language equivalents that carry the same meaning (source frames this as 'zero cognitive friction' for both average and advanced readers).
Break long sentences into short paragraphs and short lines, since pacing is part of legibility, not decoration.
Re-check each block: could a distracted scroller get the meaning in one pass without re-reading? If not, cut or simplify.
Apply the same pass to headlines and the first line of body copy, which carry the most weight.
caveats: This is the source's stated principle for direct-response legibility, not a measured conversion benchmark.

cards.title: Structure every asset around the Rule of One
cards.summary: Anchor each ad, page or email to one big idea, one reader, and one core action to avoid scattered messaging.
cards.use_when: Planning an ad, advertorial or landing page and deciding what the single job of the asset is before drafting.
steps: Name the one big idea the asset communicates — if you can't state it in a sentence, the asset will ramble.
Name the one reader: describe the specific person and situation the copy speaks to, not a broad demographic.
Name the one core action you want them to take (click, add to cart, subscribe) and remove competing calls-to-action.
Use this as a filter: any line, proof point or feature that doesn't support the one idea/reader/action is a candidate for cutting.
The source calls the failure mode 'tossed salad copy' — disparate points jumbled together with no central message; keep messages crisp and centralized.
caveats: The Rule of One is the source's framework for short- and long-form direct response; it is opinion, not a universal law.

cards.title: Apply the four-part conversion formula to any asset
cards.summary: A structural formula for ads, pages and emails: grab attention, keep it consumable, shift beliefs with proof, then drive one specific action.
cards.use_when: Drafting or rebuilding a hero section, ad, VSL script or email and needing a repeatable structure that maps to how buyers move.
steps: Grab attention past the internal spam filter — lead with something the reader hasn't already tuned out; assume their default is to ignore selling language.
Make the content consumable: pacing, short paragraphs, and legible copy so they keep reading instead of bouncing.
Shift beliefs using storytelling and proof — analogies, statistics, and cost narration (framing what the alternative costs them) rather than bare claims.
Drive immediate action with one specific call-to-action, not several.
Sequence matters: attention before belief before action; a CTA on an unconvinced reader underperforms.
caveats: The source presents this as a foundational direct-response framework; treat the sequence as a drafting structure, not a guaranteed conversion lift.

cards.title: Use Challenge/Justify/Need to break a held belief
cards.summary: A framework that confronts the buyer's existing belief, justifies an alternative, then establishes why they need it now.
cards.use_when: Running or writing ads and pages for a product that competes against a fixed customer belief, a category norm, or a 'that's just how it is' assumption.
steps: Challenge: state the commonly held belief your customer currently acts on, and directly question it — this creates the opening.
Justify: give the reasoning, mechanism or evidence for why the old belief doesn't hold, so the challenge doesn't read as empty contrarianism.
Need: connect the reframe to why the customer needs your solution specifically, now.
Apply it to a belief that actually blocks the purchase — not a cosmetic positioning angle.
Pair with a unique mechanism so the 'need' lands on your product's differentiated feature rather than a generic claim.
caveats: Challenging a deeply held belief can polarize; the source's use case is direct response to a defined avatar, not broad brand building.

cards.title: Use Problem/Agitate/Solution to build offer tension
cards.summary: A three-beat structure that names the customer's problem, intensifies the cost of leaving it, then presents the offer.
cards.use_when: Writing a paid social ad, landing page block, or email for a product that solves an acute, already-felt pain point.
steps: Problem: name the pain in the customer's own language so they recognize it immediately.
Agitate: expand on the consequences — what the problem costs them in money, time, or status if unresolved — before mentioning any product.
Solution: present your product or offer as the resolution, with proof and a specific CTA.
Keep agitation rooted in the customer's real experience; invented or exaggerated pain destroys trust in the solution.
Works best when the problem is already top-of-mind; for unaware audiences, lead with a hook before the problem statement (see HSO).
caveats: The source frames PAS as a tool to agitate pain before introducing an offer; over-agitation is a tone risk the framework doesn't self-limit.

cards.title: Use Hook/Story/Offer to ground claims in proof
cards.summary: A structure that opens with a strong hook, supports claims with a personal or case-study story, then delivers the offer.
cards.use_when: Writing advertorials, VSLs, or paid social ads where you need proof of concept grounded in a concrete narrative rather than raw claims.
steps: Hook: open with the single line or visual that earns the next second of attention.
Story: use a personal or case-study narrative that shows the transformation or outcome, so the claim is demonstrated rather than asserted.
Offer: after the story has built belief, present the offer, USP and guarantee.
Match the story type to available evidence — a customer case study, a founder story, or a documented test — don't fabricate narrative proof.
Keep the through-line on the Rule of One: the story must serve the one big idea, not become its own tangent.
caveats: The source pairs HSO with proof of concept; results depend on the strength of the underlying story, not the structure alone.

cards.title: Differentiate a product with a unique mechanism
cards.summary: Give the product a specific differentiated feature or mechanism so it escapes comparison as a generic commodity.
cards.use_when: Selecting or merchandising a product whose category is crowded and where the offer currently reads as interchangeable with competitors.
steps: Identify the concrete ingredient, technology, process or design feature that distinguishes the product — the source's example is a V12 engine versus a generic engine.
Name and explain that mechanism in the copy so the buyer evaluates your product on its own terms rather than on category price.
Place the mechanism early enough to pre-empt price comparison, and tie the mechanism to a benefit the customer cares about.
Use it in the offer: the mechanism becomes the reason the product costs what it costs.
Audit existing PDPs and ads for generic commodity language and replace it with the specific mechanism.
caveats: The unique mechanism must be a real product feature; inventing one is a false-advertising risk the source doesn't discuss.

cards.title: Architect a video sales letter (VSL) and matching page text
cards.summary: A sequence for structuring VSL scripts and their corresponding landing page blocks, from audience call-out through risk-reversed offer.
cards.use_when: Producing a VSL or a video-led landing page for a product launch or evergreen offer.
steps: Open with an audience call-out so the right viewer self-selects in the first seconds.
Identify an urgent problem early, to justify continued watching.
Throw stones at alternatives — critique competitor approaches or the status quo so your mechanism looks like the departure.
Introduce the unique mechanism or solution as the answer to the critique.
Layer in borrowed authority and statistics to support the claim without making the presenter the only proof.
Close with a risk-reversed guarantee or a clear USP so the action feels safe.
Mirror the same beats in the landing page text blocks beside the video, so skimmers get the same sequence.
caveats: This is the source's VSL architecture, not a guaranteed script; competitor critique ('throwing stones') carries legal and platform-policy risk that the source does not address — verify claims before publishing.

cards.title: Avoid 'tossed salad copy' in ads and pages
cards.summary: If every point and benefit is thrown in without a central message, the asset loses the reader — keep messaging crisp and centralized.
cards.use_when: Editing an existing ad, PDP or landing page that underperforms and feels like a list of features and claims.
steps: Read the asset and try to state its one big idea in a sentence; if you can't, that's the diagnosis.
Find the lines, proof points and features that don't support that idea, and cut or move them to a different asset.
Check the reader: is the copy written to one avatar, or is it hedging toward several at once?
Check the action: are there multiple CTAs competing for the same click?
Rewrite around the surviving central message, with the other points demoted to supporting detail.
caveats: This is the source's own term for scattered messaging; it is an editorial heuristic rather than a measured defect.

cards.title: Match copy structure to the reader's stage of awareness
cards.summary: Use frameworks in the order the audience's awareness demands — hook for unaware, problem/agitate for problem-aware, offer for solution-aware.
cards.use_when: Choosing which ad or landing page structure to run for a cold, warm or retargeting audience on paid social.
steps: Identify what the audience already knows before picking a framework: unaware of the problem, aware of the problem, aware of solutions, aware of your product.
For unaware or cold audiences, lead with Hook/Story/Offer, since the pain isn't being felt yet.
For problem-aware audiences, Problem/Agitate/Solution works because the pain is already recognized and can be intensified.
For audiences that hold a competing belief or default solution, Challenge/Justify/Need can open the door.
Apply the Rule of One and the four-part conversion formula on top of whichever framework you choose — they are structural, not stage-specific.
Test the same offer under different frameworks for different audience stages rather than assuming one structure fits all placements.
caveats: Stage-of-awareness mapping is the source's guidance for ad messaging; it is a strategic overlay, not a media-buying rule (bidding and attribution map to ad deployment, not this framework).

cards.title: Build proof into copy with analogies, stats and cost narration
cards.summary: Use three proof devices to shift beliefs: analogy to make the unfamiliar concrete, statistics for credibility, and cost narration to frame the alternative's price.
cards.use_when: Writing the belief-shift section of an ad, advertorial or landing page where claims alone aren't landing.
steps: Analogy: compare the product's mechanism or benefit to something the reader already understands, so an unfamiliar feature becomes graspable.
Statistics: cite specific supporting numbers; use real figures you can source.
Cost narration: state what the alternative, the status quo or the problem actually costs the customer, so your price is judged against that.
Place proof after the attention-grabbing opening and before the CTA, mapping to the 'shift beliefs' step of the conversion formula.
Borrow authority where useful, but keep the proof tied to the one big idea so it doesn't become a second message.
caveats: Statistics and cost figures must be verifiable; the source assumes proof is available rather than invented.

cards.title: Keep email copy to the three proven structures
cards.summary: Apply CJN, PAS or HSO as the organizing structure for each marketing email so it does one job with one arc.
cards.use_when: Writing campaign, launch, or lifecycle emails for an ecommerce list where each send needs a single persuasive arc.
steps: Pick the structure that fits the goal: CJN when you need to break a belief, PAS when the pain is already felt, HSO when you need proof via story.
Keep the email on the Rule of One: one big idea, one reader, one action.
Write legibly — short paragraphs and simple language — because pacing is part of whether it gets read.
Where a claim is strong, back it with proof devices (analogy, stat, cost narration) rather than assertion.
End with one specific CTA; don't split attention across multiple offers in the same send.
caveats: The source presents these as proven direct-response structures, not as tested email benchmarks; results depend on list, offer and deliverability.
